{{short description|Tool for assessing quality of non-randomized studies}}
In [[statistics]], the '''Newcastle–Ottawa scale''' '''(NOS)''' is a tool used for assessing the quality of non-randomized studies included in a [[systematic review]] and/or [[meta-analysis|meta-analyses]]. Using the tool, each study is judged on eight items, categorized into three groups: the selection of the study groups; the comparability of the groups; and the ascertainment of either the exposure or outcome of interest for case-control or cohort studies respectively. Stars awarded for each quality item serve as a quick visual assessment. Stars are awarded such that the highest quality studies are awarded up to nine stars. The method was developed as a collaboration between the [[University of Newcastle (Australia)|University of Newcastle, Australia]], and the [[University of Ottawa]], Canada, using a [[Delphi method|Delphi process]] to define variables for data extraction. The scale was then tested on systematic reviews and further refined.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Deeks JJ, Dinnes J, D'Amico R, Sowden AJ, Sakarovitch C, Song F, etal|year=2003|title=Evaluating non-randomised intervention studies|journal=[[Health Technology Assessment (journal)|Health Technology Assessment]]|volume=7|issue=27|pages=iii-x, 1–173 |doi=10.3310/hta7270|pmid=14499048 |doi-access=free|hdl=11380/608193|hdl-access=free}}</ref> Separate tools were developed for cohort and case–control studies. It has also been adapted for prevalence studies.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rotenstein|first1=Lisa S.|last2=Ramos|first2=Marco A.|last3=Torre|first3=Matthew|last4=Segal|first4=J. Bradley|last5=Peluso|first5=Michael J.|last6=Guille|first6=Constance|last7=Sen|first7=Srijan|last8=Mata|first8=Douglas A.|date=2016-12-06|title=Prevalence of Depression, Depressive Symptoms, and Suicidal Ideation Among Medical Students: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis|journal=JAMA|volume=316|issue=21|pages=2214–2236|doi=10.1001/jama.2016.17324|issn=1538-3598|pmid=27923088|pmc=5613659}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | author = [[Douglas A. Mata]], [[Marco A. Ramos]], [[Narinder Bansal]], [[Rida Khan]], [[Constance Guille]], [[Emanuele Di Angelantonio]] & [[Srijan Sen]] | title = Prevalence of Depression and Depressive Symptoms Among Resident Physicians: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis | journal = [[JAMA (journal)|JAMA]] | volume = 314 | issue = 22 | pages = 2373–2383 | year = 2015 | doi = 10.1001/jama.2015.15845 | pmid = 26647259 | pmc=4866499}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rotenstein|first1=Lisa S.|last2=Torre|first2=Matthew|last3=Ramos|first3=Marco A.|last4=Rosales|first4=Rachael C.|last5=Guille|first5=Constance|last6=Sen|first6=Srijan|last7=Mata|first7=Douglas A.|date=September 18, 2018|title=Prevalence of Burnout Among Physicians: A Systematic Review|journal=JAMA|volume=320|issue=11|pages=1131–1150|doi=10.1001/jama.2018.12777|issn=1538-3598|pmc=6233645|pmid=30326495}}</ref>

Strengths of the Newcastle–Ottawa scale are is that it is relatively quick to use, and its questions can be adapted to the study domain. However, there has been shown to be low levels in agreement when multiple reviewers use the Newcastle–Ottawa scale to assess studies.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Luchini |first1=Claudio |last2=Stubbs |first2=Brendon |last3=Solmi |first3=Marco |last4=Veronese |first4=Nicola |date=2017-08-26 |title=Assessing the quality of studies in meta-analyses: Advantages and limitations of the Newcastle Ottawa Scale |journal=World Journal of Meta-Analysis |language=en |volume=5 |issue=4 |pages=80–84 |doi=10.13105/wjma.v5.i4.80|doi-access=free }}</ref>

A 2019 study of systematic reviews of healthcare interventions found the Newcastle–Ottawa scale to be the most commonly used risk-of-bias tool to assess non-randomized studies in systematic reviews that used multiple risk of bias tools.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Farrah |first1=Kelly |last2=Young |first2=Kelsey |last3=Tunis |first3=Matthew C. |last4=Zhao |first4=Linlu |date=2019-11-15 |title=Risk of bias tools in systematic reviews of health interventions: an analysis of PROSPERO-registered protocols |journal=Systematic Reviews |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=280 |doi=10.1186/s13643-019-1172-8 |doi-access=free |issn=2046-4053 |pmc=6857304 |pmid=31730014}}</ref>
